title: Children and Gender Inequality: Evidence from Denmark
research_question: How does the arrival of children affect the labor market trajectories of women relative to men, and how much of overall gender inequality in earnings can be attributed to parenthood? Additionally, are the career consequences of motherhood transmitted across generations through the family environment in which women grew up?
data_description: The study uses Danish administrative register data covering the full population from 1980 to 2013, with supplementary data extending back to 1964 for the intergenerational analysis. Multiple registers are linked at the individual level via personal identification numbers, allowing researchers to connect family members across three generations and link workers with firms. Key variables include annual earnings, labor force participation, hours worked (measured in 37 discrete steps from mandatory ATP pension contributions), wage rates (earnings divided by hours), occupation, sector (public/private), firm characteristics, education level and field, and wealth. The core estimation sample consists of approximately 470,000 first births occurring between 1985 and 2003, yielding roughly 15,040,000 individual-year observations, with parents observed annually from five years before to ten years after their first child's birth. The unit of observation is the individual-year.
institutional_context: Denmark is often viewed as a frontrunner in gender equality, featuring one of the world's highest female labor force participation rates (around 80 percent) and minimal gender gaps in participation. The institutional environment combines high effective tax rates on labor with generous family policies designed to support working mothers: universally available, heavily subsidized public child care from roughly 6–12 months after birth, and job-protected paid maternity and parental leave. Until 2001, parents received 14 weeks of maternity leave plus 10 weeks of shared parental leave; from 2002, this expanded to 18 weeks of maternity leave and 32 weeks of parental leave. Throughout the sample period, families transitioned seamlessly from paid leave to subsidized child care with no coverage gap. Despite these supportive policies and relatively egalitarian gender norms, a substantial gender earnings gap of 15–20 percent persists, comparable to that in the United States, motivating examination of why parenthood continues to differentially affect women's careers.

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.identification_strategy: EVENT STUDY — treatment = mothers, control = fathers; shock/instrument/cutoff = childbirth
_legacy_v1_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The arrival of children leads to a significant and persistent child penalty for mothers: their earnings, employment, and hours decline sharply relative to fathers after childbirth and do not recover. This child penalty accounts for most of the observed gender earnings gap in Denmark.
_legacy_v1_ground_truth.main_effect: ~20% earnings decline for mothers relative to fathers within 5 years of first child
